difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: two directly linked concepts (BFS/DFS as reachability and the effect of reversing edges), with each of the four statements settled by a short argument or a two-vertex counterexample; about 2 minutes.
stem:
Consider a directed graph $G = (V, E)$, where $V$ is the finite set of vertices and $E$ is the set of directed edges between the vertices. $G$ may contain cycles but there is no self-loop. Further, $G$ may not be strongly connected.

Let $G^R$ be the graph obtained by reversing the directions of all the edges in $G$ without changing the set of vertices.

Assume that Breadth First Search (BFS) or Depth First Search (DFS) from any given vertex $v$ of a graph visits only the reachable vertices from $v$ in that graph.

Which of the following statements must always be true, regardless of the structure of $G$?

options.label: A
options.text: If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^R$ from $v$, then $u$ is also a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.

options.label: B
options.text: In $G^R$, the BFS traversal from $v$ will visit exactly the same set of vertices as the DFS from $v$ in $G$.

options.label: C
options.text: The order of vertices visited in the BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ is the reverse of the order of vertices visited in the DFS of $G$ from $v$.

options.label: D
options.text: If $u$ is a reachable vertex in the DFS of $G$ from $v$, then $v$ is also a reachable vertex in the BFS of $G^R$ from $u$.

solution.quick:
BFS and DFS from a vertex visit exactly the vertices reachable from it, so only reachability matters. Reversing every edge reverses every path: $v \leadsto u$ in $G$ $\iff$ $u \leadsto v$ in $G^R$.

That is statement (D). A two-vertex graph with one edge ($u \to v$ for (A); $v \to u$ for (B) and (C)) breaks the other three statements. **(D)**

steps.title: Concept: what BFS and DFS visit
steps.body:
By the stated assumption, BFS or DFS started at a vertex $s$ of a graph $H$ visits exactly the set

$$
\mathrm{Reach}_H(s) = \{\, x : \text{there is a directed path } s \leadsto x \text{ in } H \,\}
$$

($s$ itself included). BFS and DFS differ only in the **order** of visiting, not in the **set** visited. So "$u$ is reachable in the BFS/DFS of $H$ from $s$" just means $u \in \mathrm{Reach}_H(s)$.

steps.title: Key fact: reversing edges reverses paths
steps.body:
Suppose $v = x_0 \to x_1 \to \dots \to x_k = u$ is a directed path in $G$. In $G^R$ each edge $x_i \to x_{i+1}$ becomes $x_{i+1} \to x_i$, so $u = x_k \to x_{k-1} \to \dots \to x_0 = v$ is a directed path in $G^R$.

The converse follows the same way because $(G^R)^R = G$. Hence

$$
u \in \mathrm{Reach}_G(v) \iff v \in \mathrm{Reach}_{G^R}(u).
$$

In words: BFS/DFS of $G^R$ from $v$ finds the vertices that can **reach** $v$ in $G$ (its ancestors). BFS/DFS of $G$ from $v$ finds the vertices $v$ can reach (its descendants).

steps.title: Check (D): it is exactly the key fact
steps.body: "$u$ is reachable in the DFS of $G$ from $v$" means $u \in \mathrm{Reach}_G(v)$. By the key fact, $v \in \mathrm{Reach}_{G^R}(u)$, so the BFS of $G^R$ from $u$ visits $v$. This holds for **every** directed graph, so (D) must always be true.

steps.title: Eliminate (A), (B), (C) with two-vertex counterexamples
steps.body:
Take $V = \{v, u\}$ with a single edge.

- **(A)** Let $G$ have the edge $u \to v$, so $G^R$ has $v \to u$. BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ visits $\{v, u\}$, but DFS of $G$ from $v$ visits only $\{v\}$ because $v$ has no outgoing edge. So $u$ is reached in $G^R$ but not in $G$, and (A) fails.
- **(B)** Let $G$ have the edge $v \to u$. DFS of $G$ from $v$ visits $\{v, u\}$. $G^R$ has only $u \to v$, so BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ visits $\{v\}$. The sets differ (descendants $\ne$ ancestors in general), and (B) fails.
- **(C)** Both traversals start at $v$, so the BFS order of $G^R$ begins with $v$, while the *reverse* of the DFS order of $G$ ends with $v$. Each vertex appears once, so the two sequences can match only if both consist of $v$ alone. With the edge $v \to u$: BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ is $(v)$, and the reversed DFS order of $G$ from $v$ is $(u, v)$. They differ, so (C) fails.

A brute-force Python check over every directed graph (no self-loops) on 2, 3 and 4 vertices and every start vertex confirms: only (D) never fails.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only statement (D) holds regardless of the structure of $G$ → **(D)**.

solution.teaching:
**Reachability is what traversals compute.** In a directed graph, $u$ is *reachable* from $v$ if there is a directed path $v \leadsto u$. BFS explores level by level with a queue, and DFS goes deep first with a stack or recursion. Both keep a "visited" set and expand every unvisited out-neighbour, so both end up visiting exactly the vertices reachable from the start. BFS and DFS therefore always visit the same **set** from the same start in the same graph. Only the **order** differs, and even the order depends on how neighbours are listed.

**The reverse (transpose) graph.** $G^R$ keeps every vertex and flips every edge $a \to b$ into $b \to a$. A walk along edges in $G$ becomes the same walk traced backwards in $G^R$. So:

- Searching $G$ from $v$ answers: *where can $v$ go?* (descendants of $v$).
- Searching $G^R$ from $v$ answers: *who can come to $v$?* (ancestors of $v$ in $G$).

These two sets are generally different. For example, in a chain $a \to b \to c$ the descendants of $b$ are $\{b, c\}$ and its ancestors are $\{a, b\}$. They coincide only in special situations, such as when all the vertices involved lie in the same strongly connected component. This is exactly the idea behind Kosaraju's strongly-connected-components algorithm, which searches both $G$ and $G^R$: a vertex lies in the SCC of $v$ iff it is both a descendant and an ancestor of $v$.

**Applying it here.** Swapping the graph ($G \leftrightarrow G^R$) must go together with swapping the endpoints ($v \leftrightarrow u$). Statement (D) does both: $u$ reachable from $v$ in $G$ implies $v$ reachable from $u$ in $G^R$. Statements (A) and (B) swap the graph but keep the same start vertex, which turns descendants into ancestors, and (C) makes a claim about visiting order that cannot hold because both orders begin at $v$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ finds the vertices that can reach $v$ in $G$, not those $v$ can reach. Counterexample: $G$ has only $u \to v$. Then $u$ is reached by BFS of $G^R$ from $v$, but DFS of $G$ from $v$ visits only $v$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The two sets are the ancestors of $v$ and the descendants of $v$ in $G$, which differ in general. Counterexample: $G$ has only $v \to u$. DFS of $G$ from $v$ visits $\{v, u\}$, while BFS of $G^R$ from $v$ visits $\{v\}$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Both traversals start at $v$, so one order begins with $v$ while the other, reversed, ends with $v$. They can agree only when nothing but $v$ is visited. With $G$ having only $v \to u$, the orders are $(v)$ versus the reversed $(u, v)$. The visited sets can differ too, as in (B).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: A path $v \leadsto u$ in $G$ read backwards is a path $u \leadsto v$ in $G^R$. So whenever DFS of $G$ from $v$ reaches $u$, BFS of $G^R$ from $u$ reaches $v$, for every graph $G$.

solution.shortcut: With a reversed graph, the graph and the start/end roles must swap **together**: $v \leadsto u$ in $G$ $\iff$ $u \leadsto v$ in $G^R$. Among the reachability statements, only one swaps both, namely (D). BFS vs DFS never changes the visited set, so that wording is a distraction.
solution.commonTrap: Assuming that reversing edges does not change what is reachable from $v$ (true for undirected or strongly connected graphs, false in general) leads to choosing (A) or (B). The BFS/DFS wording is also a distraction: the traversal type never changes the visited set, only the order.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The paper writes the reversed graph as $G^R$ (superscript R), and it is transcribed that way.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve (before reading the key): BFS/DFS visit exactly the reachable set, and a path v -> ... -> u in G read backwards is a path u -> ... -> v in G^R, so (D) always holds; (A) and (B) confuse descendants with ancestors (counterexamples: G = {u->v} for (A), G = {v->u} for (B)), and (C) fails because one order starts with v while the reversed order ends with v. The verifier's own brute force over all 3-vertex digraphs and the stored brute force over all self-loop-free digraphs on 2 to 4 vertices (every start vertex) both find counterexamples to (A), (B), (C) and none to (D). This matches official key D.
